sections.body: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following hand-written rules. You show a model many labelled examples (photos labelled 'cat' or 'dog'), and it adjusts itself to reduce mistakes.
We TRAIN on one set of data and TEST on new data the model hasn't seen. OVERFITTING is when a model memorises training data but fails on new data.
Ethics: biased data gives biased results; privacy matters; decisions about people (loans, jobs) need fairness, transparency and human oversight.

quiz.q: Why test a model on data it hasn't seen?
options: To check it works on new examples, not just memorised ones
hints: Could a model just memorise answers?
A student who memorises last year's exam answers might fail a new exam. Testing on new questions shows real understanding.
quiz.explain: Testing on unseen data shows whether the model generalises instead of memorising.

quiz.q: A hiring AI was trained on past hires who were mostly one group. What's the risk?
options: It may unfairly favour that group
hints: Models learn patterns from their data.
If you learned what 'normal' food is only from one country's cookbooks, you'd think other cuisines were odd.
quiz.explain: It may learn and repeat past bias, unfairly favouring one group.

quiz.q: A model scores 99% on its training data but only 60% on new test data. What is the most likely problem?
options: Overfitting: it memorised the training examples instead of learning general patterns
The test data must be faulty, so 99% is its true accuracy
Nothing: a high training score proves the model works
hints: Compare how it does on data it has seen with data it hasn't.
A big gap between those two scores is a warning sign the lesson names.

Worked example: a different model scores 70% on training data and 69% on test data. The scores are close, so it's doing about as well on new data as on familiar data. There's no sign of memorising, though it may need better data or a more capable model to improve overall.
quiz.explain: A large gap between training (99%) and test (60%) performance is the classic sign of overfitting: the model memorised its training examples but doesn't generalise. The test score is the more honest guide to how it will perform in real use.
